Servitor Grimoire

What a servitor is, how to build one, how to run one, how to end one. Straight from the texts, simplified. Nothing extra.

“A Servitor is an entity consciously created or generated, using evocatory techniques, to perform a task or service.” — Phil Hine, Aspects of Evocation / Condensed Chaos. In the Western tradition also called a thought-form; in Tibetan practice, a tulpa.
The scale Design — Hine Sigil — Spare Launch — Carroll Lifecycle — Brand Worked examples Feed & retire Rules Lineage — Alchemy → Jung → Servitors Banishing — LBRP Solomon — Ars Notoria Forbidden Formula Quick Casts Entry #1 — Mitsu Entry #2 — Miko Blank entry Sources

The scale

Same material, more autonomy as you go up. A servitor sits in the middle.

  • SigilOne desire, compressed into one symbol. No name, no persona, no life of its own.↓
  • ServitorOne magician builds it: name, form, sigil, one job. Semi-autonomous — it works while you don't watch.↓
  • EgregoreA servitor fed by a group instead of one person. Shared use makes it stronger and less yours.↓
  • GodformAn egregore grown large and old enough that people treat it as a god.

Two kinds of servitor (Hine): specific — built for one situation, used once; and general — built for one sphere (one job area: healing, protection, luck) and reused. General ones act like expert systems: the more tasks you give them in their sphere, the better they get at it.

Design — the Hine sequence

Phil Hine's Servitor Design Sequence, from Aspects of Evocation (essay first in Nox magazine, 1988) and Chaos Servitors: A User Guide (1991). Seven questions, in order. Answer all seven before you build anything.

Tonight: you are making one servitor — or two. Run the seven steps below once, start to finish, for one servitor. If you are making two, run them twice: a full, separate pass for each one. Each pass gets its own sphere, its own statement, its own name and sigil. Do not design two servitors in one pass.

one servitor = one pass through the steps. Two servitors = two passes.

  1. General intent — pick the sphere “Sphere” here does not mean a ball. It means the servitor's one job area — the single kind of work it does. (The ball is a different thing: that's a shape you can give it later, at Step 7.) Pick exactly one area from this list:
    • Healing — help someone recover or stay well
    • Protection — guard a person, place, or thing
    • Binding — restrain or stop something
    • Harmony — smooth out conflict, keep the peace
    • Luck — tilt the odds on one kind of chance
    • Divination — bring information, answers, signs
    • Mood — shift feelings, yours or a room's
    • Success — push one kind of goal over the line
    The list is not closed. If none of these fit, name your own single area — Hine's own examples do: GOFLOWOLFOG's sphere is traffic, and Eureka's is inspiration and creativity (both below). pick one job area only. That area then tells you which colors, scents, and symbols fit.
  2. Specific intent — write the statement One sentence that is the core of its purpose — Hine calls it the servitor's “aetheric DNA.” His example for a healing servitor: “To promote rapid recovery and health in [name].” if you can't say the job in one sentence, it's two servitors.
  3. Symbols — dress the sigil Turn the statement into a sigil (method below). Then add any symbols, colors, sounds, or scents that match the task to sharpen the program. optional decoration — the sigil alone works.
  4. Time factor — set the lifespan and the end Continuous work, or only at set times? Then decide how it ends, now, not later: either code a self-destruct into it (it ends when the task is done or the time runs out), or plan a reabsorption ritual for when you retire it. no end condition = no build.
  5. Name — give it a handle The name is how you create, power, and control it, and it builds its persona. Take it from the task, or compress the statement of intent into a mantra-like name. short, invented, and used by nobody else. ICANDOO below is one.
  6. Material base — anchor it, or don't A physical home for it: bottle, ring, crystal, small figurine. Useful for long-term servitors and for recalling it. One-shot servitors can stay free-moving with no base. A scent can be the link instead — dab the perfume on the base, inhale it at launch, and the smell becomes the activation trigger. long job → give it a base. One job, once → skip it.
  7. Shape — pick the form Any shape you can hold in your mind, from a tiny homunculus to a morphing sphere. Hine's default: visualize a featureless sphere, pulsing with energy, glowing in the task's colors, sigil impressed into it. Different use of the word: this sphere is the shape — not the job area you picked at Step 1. the ball shape is enough. Fancy forms are for memory, not power.

Sigil — the Spare method

Austin Osman Spare, The Book of Pleasure (1913). Peter Carroll and Ray Sherwin lifted it into chaos magic in 1978. This is how the statement from Step 2 becomes the glyph from Step 3.

  1. Write the intent as already true Present tense, positive. Not “I want confidence” — “I am confident in social situations.”
  2. Strip it down Remove the vowels, then remove every repeated consonant. Worked example from that sentence:
M C N F D T S L
  1. Merge the letters into one glyph Overlap, rotate, and connect the remaining letters into a single abstract mark. Simplify it until it looks like a symbol, not a word.
  2. Drop the sentence From here on you work only with the glyph. The point of the stripping: your conscious mind can't read it, so it can't argue with it or lust after the result.

Statement stripped:

draw those letters on top of each other until they become one mark.

Launch — charge, release, forget

Peter J. Carroll, Liber Null (1978) — the brief paragraph on servitors in this book is what Hine built his whole method on. Carroll's sigil rules apply directly to launching a servitor.

  1. Banish Clear the space and your head first — Carroll prefers a pentagram banishing ritual, but any ritual that empties the room and the mind does the step. quiet room, phone off, a few minutes of stillness.
  2. Build the form in your mind Visualize the shape from Step 7. Speak its name. State its one job. Impress the sigil into it. see it, name it, task it — in that order.
  3. Charge it in gnosis Carroll: a sigil is charged when the mind goes quiet in trance, or when high emotion stops normal thinking altogether. That blank, buzzing moment is when you push the form out. reach it with breath, chanting, drumming, dance, or meditation — whatever reliably gets you out of your own head.
  4. Forget it Carroll's key rule: to work, both the sigil and the desire must be banished from normal waking consciousness afterward. Thinking about it daily strangles it. launch, close the book, go do something else. Log the result when it lands, not before.

Lifecycle — the Brand method

Damon Brand, Magickal Servitors (Gallery of Magick, 2016). A second complete system — same animal, different skeleton. Brand says Vision through Living Purpose can be done in under an hour.

Stage 1 — Vision (plan all of it first)

  • Purpose — what it does. Powers — how it does it. Timing — when it acts.
  • Appearance — what it looks like. Name and the Call — its name, plus the exact words that summon it.
  • Sustenance — what feeds it. Location — where it lives when idle.
  • The Fatal Flaw — a built-in kill switch: a word, act, or flaw that ends it instantly whenever you use it. Non-negotiable in Brand's system.
  • The Sigil — drawn last, from everything above.

Stages 2–6 — the life

  1. Conception — write a statement to the servitor, addressed to it, declaring what it is.
  2. Gestation — a waiting period where it gathers power before birth. Don't rush it out half-formed.
  3. Birth — the launch ritual. Same charge-and-release mechanics as Carroll, above.
  4. Living Purpose — its working life. Call it, task it, feed it as planned in Vision.
  5. Death — when the task is complete or you call it off: use the Fatal Flaw, disperse it, done. Brand also covers retasking (rewriting the job instead of killing it) and group servitors.

David Michael Cunningham's Creating Magickal Entities (2003, with Taylor Ellwood & Amanda R. Wagener) is the third full system: same build, different vocabulary — “entity” for servitor, “programming symbol” for sigil. Full text linked in Sources.

Worked examples — from Hine's text

ICANDOO — the general servitor

  • Built by: a group of 12, in an open workshop.
  • Job: help whoever calls it overcome obstacles. The name is the job — “I can do” — and the name doubles as its summoning mantra.
  • Design trick: built to divide holographically — every user gets the whole servitor, not a slice of it.
  • Result per Hine: all 12 used it through the day on real problems.

GOFLOWOLFOG — the functional spirit

  • Job: ease traffic blockages. Sphere (job area): traffic → function: easing stoppages.
  • Name: GO FLOW, mirrored to make it barbaric — GOFLOWOLFOG.
  • Form: a shades-wearing cat on a skateboard. Sound: “Neeeowww.” Sigil: a circle with two opposite-running arrows, usable as a car talisman.
  • Character: cool, stylish, relaxed — you call him by inwardly matching that mood, ride the vision a moment, then let go.
  • Payment: let someone else move — leave a gap for a driver, step back for someone in a hurry — and be kind to the next cat you see.

Hine's point: name + form + character + one function is a complete build. You can assemble a grimoire of these with friends — the more reported successes, the more “confidence” (his word for power) the spirit gains.

Feed it, then retire it

Feeding

  • Use feeds it. Hine: every use of a servitor feeds it, and every result you credit to it boosts its power. Attribute the wins inside its sphere to it — deliberately.
  • Give it a food source at design time. Brand's Sustenance step: define what it eats — your attention at a set time, a candle, a scent, sunlight on its base. A servitor with no defined food source feeds on the nearest one: you.
  • General servitors improve with feeding. More tasks in-sphere + more credited successes = a stronger expert. That's the whole maintenance loop.

Retiring

  1. If you coded a self-destruct: it ends itself when the task completes or the time expires. Confirm and close the entry.
  2. If not — reabsorption ritual (Hine): call it back from its task, visualize taking it apart piece by piece, take back the original desire that sparked it, then destroy or dismantle its material base.
  3. Brand's servitors: trigger the Fatal Flaw built in at Vision. That's what it's for.

Hine's reason, in plain terms: retiring a finished servitor is you reclaiming responsibility for the desire you built it out of. It closes the loop psychologically as well as magically.

Rules — the short list

  • One servitor, one job. Vague intent is the failure mode in every text. Break big goals into single-task servitors.
  • Set the end before the beginning. Lifespan, completion condition, and kill method go in at design time (Hine Step 4, Brand's Fatal Flaw).
  • Feed it from something that isn't you. Define sustenance up front.
  • Don't lust for result. Charge, launch, forget (Carroll). Checking on it hourly is interference, not diligence.
  • Don't become dependent. Hine's servitor Eureka (sphere: inspiration and creativity, 1992) worked so well that when it went “offline” in 1993 he found creative thinking suddenly much harder — it had become a load-bearing part of his process. He recalled it, disassembled it, and kept only a splinter as a focus. A servitor is a tool you pick up, not a faculty you outsource.
  • It doesn't replace action. Every system assumes you also move in the ordinary world. The servitor works the odds; you still show up.

Lineage — Alchemy → Jung → Servitors

Where servitor work comes from, in one line: an old discipline for transforming material, read by Jung as a discipline for transforming the self, then rebuilt by chaos magic as a practical tool. Each step below keeps the same shape — a target form, a structured practice, held over time.

Alchemy — transmutation

Alchemy's core operation is transmutation: base material deliberately transformed into gold under a disciplined, repeated process. It is the original “success working” — state a target form, apply a structured practice, and hold that practice over time until the material changes.

pick what it should become, work it the same way, again and again, until it becomes that.

The Mellon Collection — where the manuscripts live

The Mellon Collection at Yale's Beinecke Library — Paul and Mary Mellon; Mary began collecting after meeting Carl Jung — holds more than 300 medieval and Renaissance alchemy and occult manuscripts. Most are digitized and free to read online, including Mellon MS 2 (c. 1350, practical alchemies) and the Alchemical and Rosicrucian Compendium (c. 1760). Fact note: the collection is public, not “forbidden” — that framing in a popular post is corrected here.

Yale holds the old alchemy books, Mary Mellon started the collection after meeting Jung, and anyone can read most of them online for free.

Jung — alchemy as psychology

Jung read alchemy as a psychology of transformation: the “work” on the material mirrors the work on the self. In his reading, the opus — the alchemical work — is the operator's own change, described in the language of substances, vessels, and stages.

the alchemist changing the metal was also a picture of the alchemist changing himself.

The modern end — chaos magic and servitors

Chaos magic — Spare → Carroll → Hine — turned that into servitors: a budded-off part of the psyche given one job (Hine, Condensed Chaos). A success servitor like Mitsu (Entry #1) is the practical descendant of the alchemical project: a stated form (“I am a successful manager at Mitsubishi HC Capital America”), a structured practice (scheduled feeding), held over time.

same pattern, new form — alchemy aimed at gold, Jung aimed at the self, Mitsu aimed at one stated job as a manager.

Banishing — the Lesser Banishing Ritual of the Pentagram

The Golden Dawn's clearing ritual — the LBRP. It clears the space and settles the mind before other work, and closes the space after it. The Golden Dawn taught it to Neophytes before anything else, and it is the pentagram banishing Carroll points to in the Launch section above. Performed daily, it is also a standing practice on its own. Text as published by Israel Regardie in The Golden Dawn (Vol. 1, 1937 — “The Lesser Ritual of the Pentagram,” p. 106) and in Aleister Crowley's Liber O vel Manus et Sagittae (1909). Full texts linked in Sources.

the clean-the-room ritual. Before work, after work, and once a day whether or not you work.

Part 1 — the Kabbalistic Cross

Stand facing east. Take the dagger in the right hand, or use the first two fingers. Visualize a cross of light forming on your body as you touch each point — a line of white light running head to foot, crossed at the shoulders. Vibrate each word — say it so it resonates, don't just speak it.

  1. Ateh — forehead Touch the forehead and vibrate Ateh (“Thou art”). Visualize light above the head, drawn down to that point.
  2. Malkuth — breast, pointing down Bring the hand down to the breast and point downward toward the groin and the feet, vibrating Malkuth (“the Kingdom”). The line of light runs down the body to the ground.
  3. ve-Geburah — right shoulder Touch the right shoulder and vibrate ve-Geburah (“and the Power”).
  4. ve-Gedulah — left shoulder Carry the hand across the chest to the left shoulder — tracing the crossbar of light — and vibrate ve-Gedulah (“and the Glory”).
  5. le-olam, Amen — hands clasped Clasp the hands at the breast, dagger point up between the fingers, and vibrate le-olam, Amen (“to the ages, Amen” / “for ever, Amen”).

forehead, down, right shoulder, left shoulder, hands together. Five touches, one cross of light.

Part 2 — the four quarters

At each quarter you draw the same figure: the banishing Pentagram of Earth. Draw it large, in the air, visualized in flaming blue or brilliant white light. Start at the lower-left point and draw upward to the top point — that rising first stroke is what makes it the banishing Earth figure (the invoking figure runs the current the other way). Continue: top → lower-right → upper-left → upper-right → back to the lower-left start. Then thrust the dagger (or fingers) into the center of the finished pentagram and vibrate the divine name of that quarter. Move clockwise — east, south, west, north — tracing a line of light from the center of each pentagram to the next, so the four are joined by a circle. Finish back in the east, then return to the center.

  • East — Air. Face east, draw the pentagram, vibrate YHVH (pronounced Yeh-ho-vah). Archangel of the quarter: Raphael.
  • South — Fire. Turn clockwise to the south, draw the pentagram, vibrate Adonai (Ad-oh-nye). Archangel: Michael.
  • West — Water. Turn clockwise to the west, draw the pentagram, vibrate Eheieh (Eh-hee-eh). Archangel: Gabriel.
  • North — Earth. Turn clockwise to the north, draw the pentagram, vibrate AGLA (Ahg-lah). Archangel: Uriel. Then complete the circle back to the east and return to the center, facing east.

same pentagram four times — lower-left point, up first — one name vibrated into the center of each. Walk it clockwise.

Part 3 — the archangels

Back at the center, facing east, extend the arms in the form of a cross and visualize the four archangels standing at the quarters around you — Raphael before you in the east, Gabriel behind you in the west, Michael at your right hand in the south, Uriel at your left hand in the north. Say, from Liber O:

“Before me Raphael; behind me Gabriel; on my right hand Michael; on my left hand Uriel; for about me flames the Pentagram, and in the column shines the six-rayed Star.”

arms out in a cross, four archangels at the four sides, pentagrams flaming around you, the six-rayed star in the column above and below.

Part 4 — close

Repeat the Kabbalistic Cross from Part 1, exactly as before: Ateh, Malkuth, ve-Geburah, ve-Gedulah, le-olam, Amen. The ritual ends where it began.

same cross you opened with. Open with it, close with it — nothing added.

Practical notes — from the tradition

  • Standing, facing east to start. The whole rite is done on your feet; you begin and end facing east, and every turn between quarters is clockwise.
  • Weapon: a steel dagger in the right hand in Regardie's text; Crowley says “the proper weapon (usually the Wand).” Fingers alone are the common fallback — the gesture and the visualization carry it.
  • Light: the pentagrams are visualized in flaming blue or brilliant white light, the Cross as a column and crossbar of light on the body. Hold the pictures while you move; the visualization is part of the rite, not decoration.
  • Vibrate, don't recite. The divine names and the words of the Cross are vibrated — pitched and resonant, felt in the body — in both Regardie and Crowley.
  • When: before any magical work, and again after it — Regardie: clear and consecrate the place first. Crowley in Liber O: the banishing rituals are used “at the commencement of any ceremony whatever.” As daily practice, Crowley's notes give two or three performances a day; the Golden Dawn pattern is invoking in the morning, banishing in the evening.
  • Pairing with servitor work: this is the banish in Step 1 of the Launch section, in full form — run it before a launch and after, and the space starts and ends clear.

stand, face east, turn clockwise, draw in light, vibrate the names, cross at the start and the end. Five minutes, no equipment required.

Solomon — the Ars Notoria

The oldest art in this grimoire, and the one the rest of the tradition keeps pointing back to. Ars Notoria means “the Notory Art” — the art of the notae, the figures. Its full Latin title, as Robert Turner Englished it in 1657, is Ars Notoria, quam Creator Altissimus Salomoni revelavit — “the Notory Art, which the Most High Creator revealed to Solomon.” Turner’s is the only historic English translation, and it is the text used here.

a prayer-and-picture art for knowledge, said to have been given to Solomon. Everything below is from Turner’s text and the tradition as set out in the Ars Notoria space — nothing added.

“In the Name of the Holy and undivided Trinity, beginneth this most Holy Art of Knowledge, revealed to Solomon, which the Most High Creator by his Holy Angels ministered to Solomon upon the Alter of the Temple; that thereby in short time he knew all Arts and Sciences, both Liberal and Mechanick, with all the Faculties and Properties thereof: He has suddenly infused into him, and also was filled with all wisdom, to utter the Sacred Mysteries of most Holy words.” — Opening of the treatise, Turner (1657), spelling as printed.

in plain words: the book says an angel brought this art to Solomon in the Temple, and by it he learned everything, fast, and was filled with wisdom.

What it promises — in plain words

The art promises mastery of the seven liberal arts — the whole school course of its time:

  • Grammar — writing and language, rightly used
  • Dialectic — logic: clear thinking and arguing
  • Rhetoric — eloquence: speaking well and being heard
  • Arithmetic — number
  • Music — harmony
  • Geometry — measure
  • Astronomy — the heavens

Alongside the arts, the same orations ask for four things the text names together again and again: understanding, memory, eloquence — and, in the lunation exposition, “the Faculty of Ruling those three.” Apollonius, whose prologue introduces the treatise, calls it the Flores aurei — the Golden Flowers — and the introduction is “Confirmed, Composed, and Approved by the Authority of Solomon, Manichaeus, and Euduchaeus,” in Turner’s words.

learn the seven school subjects, plus a better memory, clearer understanding, and a better way with words to run them.

How the art works — prayer, then picture

  1. Prepare first Before any oration is read or pronounced, Turner’s mandate is to rehearse the opening prayer “reverently and devoutly” first. The tradition around the text adds the preparation the Ars Notoria space sets out: confession, fasting, purity of life, and attention to the course of the Moon and the choice of days and hours. The foundation oration itself is to be said with the operator alone, secretly, “with a low voyce, so that he scarcely hear himself,” and fast on the first day he rehearses it. clean life, empty stomach on day one, alone, quiet voice, opening prayer first — every time.
  2. Pick one art — and only that art’s nota Each art has its own nota: a drawn figure of circles, compartments, divine and angelic names, and pieces of prayer, built to be looked at. Turner is explicit that the notes do not cross over: “the Note of every Art, hath not any office of transcending to another Art; neither do the Notes of one Art profit or assist to the knowledge of another Art.” one subject, one picture. The picture for speaking does not teach numbers.
  3. Say the oration for that art An oration is a prayer said out loud. Each art has its own orations, to be pronounced “as it is written,” in their due time and season. Many of the words are not translated at all — Turner says some orations “cannot be expounded nor understood, by humane sense,” being framed out of Hebrew, Greek, and Chaldee, and are to be said as written. say the prayer for that subject, out loud, as written — even the words nobody can translate.
  4. Look at the nota while you pray and study The method joins prayer to image: recite the oration while inspecting — looking closely at — the nota of the art you seek. Knowledge is expected to arrive as infusion while the mind is fixed on the figure and lifted by the prayer. One honest limit, from the Ars Notoria space: Turner printed no figures. The notae survive only in the manuscripts, so a working copy uses a manuscript figure for the subject. prayer in the ears, picture in the eyes, book open in front of you — all three at once.
  5. Repeat at the set times The foundation oration “is to be rehearsed four times a day, beginning in the morning once, about the third hour once, once in the ninth hour, and once in the evening.” The set days are days of the Moon: the 4th, 8th, 12th, 16th, 24th, and 28th in Turner’s exposition of the lunations — “say that Oration very diligently four times in those dayes.” four times a day, on the set moon-days. Repeating on a schedule is the engine, not a one-off.

Two orations worth knowing by name

  • The Queen of Tongues. “Amongst these Orations, there is more excellent than the rest, which King Solomon would therefore have be called, The Queen of Tongues because it takes away, as it were, with a certain Secret covering the Impediments of the Tongue, and giveth it a marvellous Faculty of Eloquence.” Turner says it is an invocation of the angels that “provoketh Eloquence, and ought to be said in the beginning of the Scripture, and in the beginning of the Moneth,” spoken secretly, with a pure mind, fasting, before meat or drink. the tongue-loosener: say it at the start of the month and before reading, alone and fasting, when you need your words to come out right.
  • Assaylemath — the Splendor, or Speculum, of Wisdom. “Assaylemath, Assay, Lemath, Azzabue” — the oration of the four tongues (Chaldee, Greek, Hebrew, and Latin) that Solomon left without an exposition, because, Turner says, no man could attain to its perfection. Said at the appointed lunations, the text promises it “increaseth thy Memory, Understanding, Eloquence, and establisheth them all in thee.” Apollonius calls this kind of oration “The Light of the Soul, and the Speculum of Wisdom”; Solomon calls it “The happiness of Wit.” the one nobody is allowed to explain. You just say it, on the set days, for memory, understanding, and eloquence.

The worked example the book itself gives — rhetoric

Rhetoric’s figures divide a speech into the parts it must have, so the figure teaches the art it belongs to: Exordium (the opening that wins the hearer) · Narratio (the facts) · Partitio (the plan) · Confirmatio (the proof) · Reprehensio (answering objections) · … · Finis (the close). The third figure of rhetoric is that map drawn as a wheel of text and angels.

open strong, state the facts, show the plan, prove it, answer the pushback, close clean. That is the whole speech, in one picture.

The other verdict — kept on the record

The tradition also carries its condemnation, and this grimoire keeps it next to the art, as the Ars Notoria space does. Thomas Aquinas, in the Summa Theologiae (II–II, q. 96, a. 1), judged the notory art “both unlawful and futile”: a drawn figure cannot teach grammar by any natural power, and God never instituted these signs as He instituted the sacraments — so, in his argument, the signs can only work as tokens of a pact. John of Morigny’s early-1300s attempt to rewrite the method around the Virgin Mary, the Liber florum, was condemned and publicly burned at Paris in 1323. The books were copied anyway, for centuries.

the Church said no, burned the reformed version in 1323, and people kept copying the art regardless. Know both halves before you work it.

The Forbidden Formula — withdrawal, trace, and speech

From the Instagram carousel “Forbidden Formula” by @madalina__666, posted Nov 7, 2026 — five slides, read in full. The teaching underneath the title is Kabbalistic, drawn from Lurianic Kabbalah: how creation makes room, what is left behind when the Light pulls back, and why speech is not just talk. Stated plainly below, slide by slide, with the honest notes kept next to it.

View the carousel on Instagram →

The core teaching — Ein Sof, Tzimtzum, Reshimu

Ein Sof — the Infinite Without End — filled everything. With everything full, there was no room for a world. So creation began with Tzimtzum: a divine Withdrawal, a contraction, that made room for a world to exist in. The withdrawal was itself an act of Speech — “And God said.” And what remained in the hollow the withdrawal left was Reshimu — the Trace: the residue, the memory of Light after Light withdraws. The world itself is this Trace, and language is how the Trace becomes legible.

first there was only the Infinite; it pulled back to make room, and the world is what the Light left behind — words are how you read it.

The Echo That Cannot Be Grasped

True speech is participation in creation, not mere communication. The carousel quotes the Zohar:

“No thought can grasp Him completely”

The Real is inexhaustible, so every true utterance is a departure, not an arrival — you speak toward it knowing the speaking will not finish it. Silence is the ground of the word, not its enemy. The post frames this as the “Thirty-Two Apostillas”: each one an echo reaching toward the Real, knowing it will not arrive.

you never say the whole thing. A true word is a reaching, not a capturing — and it starts from silence, not against it.

The Silence Before the Word — Theolinguistics

Silence is the source and the end of speech. Language is where three lines converge:

  • The Real — what is
  • Reality — what appears
  • Consciousness — what perceives

Language emanates from Silence and returns to it. The word comes out of the quiet and goes back to the quiet; the quiet is not empty — it is where the word comes from.

silence first, word second, silence again after. Language is where what is, what appears, and what perceives meet.

Before you speak a thing into being, make room — withdraw, sit in the silence, then let the word leave a trace.

What’s real / what’s packaging

  • Real: Ein Sof, Tzimtzum, and Reshimu are genuine concepts from Lurianic Kabbalah — the system of Isaac Luria, 16th century. The carousel did not invent them.
  • No technique in the slides: the carousel contains no step-by-step technique. The “formula” is never spelled out as steps in the slides — what is there is the teaching above, not a procedure.
  • The buried paper is unverified: the closing slide — “They buried this paper for decades. I tracked down the entire document” — is a gate to a paid document, “Document 01: The Forbidden Formula,” sold via the Gumroad link in the author’s bio. No paper title, author, or source is named, so the buried-paper claim is unverified.
  • Labeled AI content: Instagram labels the post as AI content.

Quick Casts — minutes, not hours

The short ones. Each of these takes minutes, right before the thing you are about to do, and mirrors the Quick Casts in the Ars Notoria space. Every set of words below is copied from Turner’s text, in his spelling — nothing here is made up. Each cast is marked from the text or modern version: “from the text” means Turner says to do it; “modern version” means the idea is his and the short form is fitted to normal life now. Plain numbered steps, and one simple line under each.

1. The one-line opening

From the text  Time: 1 minute · You need: nothing

For: starting anything — study, work, a hard task.

“The Light, Truth, Life, Way, Judge, Mercy, Fortitude and Patience, preserve, help me, and have Mercy upon me, Amen.”

In plain words: a one-line ask for light, truth, strength, patience, and mercy before you begin. Turner puts it at the start of the first grammar picture.

  1. Stop. Phone down, one breath.
  2. Say the line out loud, slowly, once.
  3. Start the task right away, while the words are still in your head.

one line, said once, then start. No setup.

2. Morning words before hard reading

From the text  Time: 2 minutes · You need: the text you are about to read

For: a text you have to understand — a contract, a manual, scripture, study notes.

“Hely Scemath”

Two words the book never translates — it says some of its words are too deep to put into plain language, and to say them as written. Turner pairs them with a prayer that starts “Theos Megale” — Greek for “Great God.” His direction: pronounce them “in the morning betimes of that day, wherein thou wilt begin any work,” then “diligently pronounce the Scripture proposed.”

  1. Do this early in the morning, before you start — first thing.
  2. Say “Hely Scemath” out loud, once, slowly.
  3. Then read your text out loud, carefully, one time through. Do not skim.

two untranslated words at dawn, then read the hard thing out loud, slowly, once.

3. The memory line

From the text  Time: 1–2 minutes · You need: the thing you want to remember

For: right before something you must not forget — a name, a list, a talk.

“Adorn my Soul, that hearing I may hear; and what I hear, I may retain in my Memory.”

In plain words: “Let me really hear this — and keep it.” One line from the book’s long prayer for a good memory, which Turner says to say in the morning if it is for memory.

  1. Say the line out loud once.
  2. Read or listen to the thing once, with full attention — nothing else going on.
  3. Say the line once more, then close the book and say the thing back in your own words.

line, listen once with everything you have, line again, say it back from memory.

4. Before you have to speak

From the text  Time: 1 minute · You need: a moment alone

For: a call, a meeting, a presentation, a tough conversation.

“Omnipotent and merciful Father… I beseech thee to illuminate my heart this day… that I may understand and know what I desire, and what things are considerable to be known in this Art, Amen.”

The short prayer Turner puts before the first rhetoric picture — rhetoric is the art of speaking well. In plain words: “Clear my head today, so I know what matters and can say it.”

  1. Step away alone for one minute before you go in.
  2. Say the prayer out loud, once.
  3. Name, in one sentence, the one point you most need to get across. Then go.

Turner’s own count for his big eloquence oration, if you want more of it: repeat it once and “Eloquence shall be added to thee, as much as is needed”; twice, and “great Eloquence shall be given to thee”; three times, to be made eloquent.

one minute alone, one prayer, one point to land. Once, twice, or three times — that is Turner’s scale.

5. The numbers prayer

From the text  Time: 1 minute · You need: the numbers in front of you

For: math, money, budgets, measuring — anything with numbers.

“Oh God who numbrest, weighest, and measurest all things… Grant the knowledge of this Art unto my understanding, that I may love thee, and acknowledge the gift of thy goodness, Amen.”

Turner’s prayer before the first arithmetic picture. In plain words: “You count and measure everything — help me understand this.”

  1. Put the numbers in front of you — the bill, the budget, the problem.
  2. Say the prayer out loud, once.
  3. Work through the numbers slowly, one line at a time, checking each as you go.

numbers open, prayer once, then one line at a time and check each one.

6. The two-minute picture gaze

Modern version  Time: 2 minutes · You need: one nota picture (manuscript figures — Turner printed none)

For: focus, when your head is scattered and you need it on one thing.

The full version in the book is long — the same picture looked at many times a day, for days. This is the short form, fitted to normal life now:

  1. Open the picture for your subject full-screen, or set the printed page in front of you.
  2. Set a timer for two minutes. Look slowly around the circles. Follow the lines. Breathe slow.
  3. When the timer ends, close your eyes for ten seconds and picture it once more. Then start your work.

two quiet minutes on one picture, eyes closed for ten seconds, then work.

7. For vanity — presence, and how you are received

From the text  Time: 2–3 minutes · You need: a moment alone, before you go in

For: walking into a room, a meeting, a first impression — how you come across, and how people take your words.

First, the honest limit, in plain words: the text has no working to change your face or your body, and none is invented here. What it does have — in quantity — is eloquence: words that land, and a presence hearers receive well. That is the vanity the book can actually speak to, and this cast uses only that. Its words are from Turner’s oration “for Eloquence and stability of mind”:

“Lift up the senses of my Heart and Soul unto thee, Oh Lord my God, and elevate my heart this day unto thee; that my words and works may please thee in the sight of all people… let thy Holy Eloquence be sweet in my mouth, that what I read or hear I may understand and repeat…”

A second line from the same part of the book asks for the receiving end of it: “give me Eloquence, Learning, and Knowledge, that those that shall hear my words, they may be mellifluous in their Hearts; that seeing and hearing thy wisdome, the proud may be made humble, and hear and understand my words…” In plain words: “Let my words and my work look and sound right to the people in front of me — and let what I say go down sweet with the people who hear it.”

  1. Do the ordinary part first — this grimoire’s standing rule is that no working replaces action. Get ready the way you actually want to be seen: clothes, hair, posture, on time.
  2. Step alone for a moment, the way Turner’s orations are said: secretly, in a low voice, so you can scarcely hear yourself.
  3. Say the words above out loud, slowly, once.
  4. If you want Turner’s full scale for eloquence, use his count from Cast 4: say the oration once for eloquence as needed, twice for great eloquence, three times to be made eloquent.
  5. Name, in one sentence, how you want to come across in there — calm, sharp, warm, in charge. Then go in and do that part yourself.

look the part in the real world first, then the low-voice line that asks for your words and works to please in the sight of all people. The book works the reception; you work the entrance.

One rule runs under all seven, from Turner and from this grimoire alike: a cast does not replace the ordinary work. The prayer, the quiet, and the picture are the method — you still open the book, run the numbers, and walk into the room yourself.

say the words, then go do the thing. Both halves, every time.

Entry #1 — Mitsu

Launched Nov 12, 2026

Your first servitor. Designed tonight, in full, before launch — sphere, statement, sigil, form, base, feeding, lifespan, and the way out all set below. Launched tonight, November 12, 2026: you performed the birth yourself — the 3-breath rite into the coin, as set out in the activation below.

  • Name Mitsu
  • Sphere (one job area) Success
  • Statement of intent “I am a successful manager at Mitsubishi HC Capital America”
  • Job limits Mitsu works only on my performance, presence, and judgment as a manager at Mitsubishi HC Capital America — nothing outside that lane.
  • Sigil Drawn by hand from the statement, Spare method. The letters it was built from:
    M S C F L N G R T B H P
    the hand-drawn glyph is the sigil. These letters are just its ingredients — work with the glyph, not the sentence.
  • Form A sphere, visualized in your head, with the sigil impressed into it — Hine's default form. The sphere is the shape in your mind; the coin below is where it lives in the physical world. sphere in the head, coin in the hand.
  • Material base / location The Memento Mori coin — Mitsu's physical home and anchor. Hold the coin whenever you activate, feed, task, or dismiss Mitsu.
  • Feeding Daily at 6:33 AM — breathe into the coin 7 times. Same feed, every day, on schedule — not extra when results come in, not skipped when they don't. 7 breaths into the coin, daily at 6:33 AM. That's the whole feeding rite.
  • Lifespan Continuous — Mitsu works on an ongoing basis until you retire.
  • End condition Retirement ends it. Before that, the Fatal Flaw below ends it early, any time you choose.
  • Fatal Flaw / kill method Built in now, before launch: hold the coin, speak Mitsu's name and that its work is done, then breathe out over the coin 7 times — the feeding reversed — and never feed it again. It reabsorbs. feeding reversed = dismissal. Out-breath ×7, name spoken, work declared done, no more feeding.
  • Date launched November 12, 2026 — launched tonight with the 3-breath birth into the coin (see activation below).
  • Results log — nothing logged yet. Log a result when it lands, not before.
  • Retired — no. Runs until you retire, or until you use the Fatal Flaw.

Mitsu — Sealed Sigil

This sigil is sealed. It stays hidden until you unseal it.

Activation — the birth, with the coin

Done once, by you, at launch — performed November 12, 2026. Kept here as the record of how Mitsu was born. This follows the Launch section above (Carroll), with the coin as the anchor:

  1. Settle and hold the coin Quiet room, phone off, a few minutes of stillness. Hold the Memento Mori coin — Mitsu's base — in your hand. coin in hand, head clear.
  2. Build the sphere Visualize the sphere in your head, sigil impressed into it, glowing in its task's colors. see the sphere, see the sigil in it.
  3. Speak the name and the statement Speak the name — Mitsu — then state the one job, the statement of intent: “I am a successful manager at Mitsubishi HC Capital America.” Keep it inside the job limits above — performance, presence, and judgment as a manager at Mitsubishi HC Capital America, nothing outside that lane. name it, then task it — in that order.
  4. Breathe into the coin — 3 times Breathe into the coin 3 times. That is the birth: the charge goes into the sphere in your head and anchors in the coin in your hand. 3 breaths in = born. (Feeding later is 7 — don't mix them up.)
  5. Release and forget Put the coin down and away, close the book, go do something else. Don't check on it or rehearse it daily — per Carroll, lusting for result strangles it. The daily feeding below is a feed, not a check-in. launch it, then leave it alone to work.

After launch — the daily rhythm

  • Feed daily at 6:33 AM: hold the coin, breathe into it 7 times — at 6:33 AM, daily. That's the fixed time; holding it at 6:33 AM is the habit that makes it hold. Nothing else is required at a feeding — no statement, no checking for results.
  • To task it: hold the coin, speak the name, give it one task inside its lane, visualize the sphere with its sigil a moment — then let go and get on with your own part of the work. It doesn't replace action: Mitsu works the odds, you still show up.
  • Credit the wins: when something inside its lane goes right, attribute it to Mitsu in the results log above. Per Hine, credited successes are what make a general servitor stronger.

Ending Mitsu — retirement and the early exit

  • At retirement: Mitsu's lifespan ends. Close it out with the same dismissal rite below, note the date in this entry, and the loop is closed.
  • Early, any time — the Fatal Flaw: hold the coin, speak Mitsu's name and that its work is done, breathe out over the coin 7 times — the feeding reversed — and never feed it again. Visualize the sphere coming apart and the desire returning to you as you do it. Done: it reabsorbs.

in ×3 = birth · in ×7 daily at 6:33 AM = feeding · out ×7 = the end. All three run through the coin.

Sources — direct links to the texts

  • Aspects of Evocation — Phil Hine
    Collected essays, 1988–95. Contains the “Servitors” essay, the full Design Sequence, ICANDOO, GOFLOWOLFOG, and the Eureka warning. This page's core source.
    Read the full text (PDF) →
  • Liber Null & Psychonaut — Peter J. Carroll
    Revised & expanded edition, Weiser Books, 2022 (original Liber Null, 1978). Sigils, gnosis, evocation — and the paragraph that started servitor work.
    Read the full text (Archive.org) →
  • Magickal Servitors — Damon Brand
    The Gallery of Magick, 2016. The Vision → Conception → Gestation → Birth → Living Purpose → Death system, including the Fatal Flaw.
    Read the full text (Archive.org) →
  • Creating Magickal Entities — David Michael Cunningham, with Taylor Ellwood & Amanda R. Wagener
    Egregore Publishing, 2003. The only book-length system devoted entirely to entity creation.
    Read the full text (PDF) →
  • Sigil-Making: History, Theory, and Method — Grimoire
    Spare's method laid out clean: statement, strip repeats, merge into glyph, charge, forget. Source for the worked letter example above.
    Read the method →
  • Creating Magickal Entities — review, Spiral Nature Magazine
    Independent review of the Cunningham system — useful check on how it differs from chaos-magick terminology.
    Read the review →
  • Phil Hine — Wikipedia
    Bibliography and background: Chaos Servitors: A User Guide (1991), Condensed Chaos (1992 / New Falcon 1995), Prime Chaos.
    Open the page →
  • The Golden Dawn, Vol. 1 — Israel Regardie
    Aries Press, 1937. “The Lesser Ritual of the Pentagram” at p. 106 — the Golden Dawn text of the LBRP above: Kabbalistic Cross, the four quarters, and the uses of the ritual. Vol. 3 (1939) carries the expanded “Ritual of the Pentagram.”
    Read the full text (Archive.org) →
  • Liber O vel Manus et Sagittae — Aleister Crowley
    The Equinox I(2), 1909; also in Magick, Book 4. Crowley's numbered text of the Lesser Ritual of the Pentagram — the source for the archangel words quoted above — plus his instructions on banishing at the start of any ceremony.
    Read the full text →
  • Lesser Ritual of the Pentagram — Wikipedia
    Overview and structure: the three parts (Qabalistic Cross, formulation of the pentagrams, evocation of the archangels), the elemental attributions, and the banishing/invoking pair.
    Open the page →
  • Ars Notoria: The Notory Art of Solomon — Robert Turner
    London, 1657. The only historic English translation — the source for the Solomon section and every Quick Cast above: the revelation to Solomon, the notae, the lunation days, the Queen of Tongues, Assaylemath, and all the orations quoted. Turner printed no figures; the notae survive only in the manuscripts. Public domain.
    Read the full text (Archive.org) →
  • Ars Notoria — Joseph H. Peterson’s edition (Grimoirer reader)
    Turner’s English with excerpts of the Agrippa Latin alongside, plus Peterson’s own introduction and notes (his copyright — linked, not copied). The reading edition behind the Ars Notoria space this material is drawn from.
    Read the edition →
  • Summa Theologiae II–II, q. 96, a. 1 — Thomas Aquinas
    The classic condemnation of the notory art quoted in the Solomon section: knowledge by discovery, instruction, or divine gift — and why, in Aquinas’s argument, the notae fall under none of them.
    Read the article (New Advent) →
